body.text: Given the many constraints of Nepal-India ties, Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s two-day visit to New Delhi could hardly have gone any better. He went with two main goals: to secure funds to rebuild the infrastructure damaged by the August floods and to get an additional air entry route via India in order to ease traffic congestion in Nepali skies.
Both these goals were met – at least on paper.

India agreed to extend an economic package worth $1.62 billion, which includes $377 million in grants for post-disaster rebuilding and a larger $1.24 billion line of credit to be spent on energy projects.

But the bigger coup for Shah was securing an air-entry route via Bhairahawa in Western Nepal. While Nepal has seven points from which aircraft can leave the country, nearly 90 percent of incoming flights enter through Simara in the east. The permission for international flights to enter Nepal through Bhairahawa is expected to ease traffic congestion significantly.

In terms of agreements, these were the two big achievements. Yet the symbolism of the trip, which lasted about 25 hours, was no less important. The Shah government had got off on the wrong foot with India, as the new Nepali prime minister declined to see the Indian foreign secretary, who was due to travel to Nepal in order to invite Shah to New Delhi. In fact, the Nepali prime minister was not meeting with any foreign official at the time, yet India still saw it as a rejection of a close friend. New Delhi also suspected that the Shah government was partial towards Western countries, especially the U.S.

With India witnessing its own youth-led protests, the political establishment in New Delhi was suspicious of Shah, a 37-year-old head of government who came to power on the back of a Gen Z protest. Internal disputes in Nepal’s ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) have also made India doubt the longevity of the Shah government.
Nonetheless, even during Shah’s short trip, there were strong signs of warmth between him and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The two were due to meet for half an hour, but ended up talking for two hours. Modi also praised Shah, hailing him as a leader with “clear vision and commitment to his country.” A long list of agreements and understandings also suggested a level of trust.

Among other things, the two prime ministers flagged off a train on a Hindu pilgrimage line between Ayodhya (India) and Janakpur (Nepal), and agreed to expedite pending hydropower projects. India granted Nepal access to two more seaports for international maritime trade. Nepal and India also put out a “joint vision statement” to chart out future bilateral cooperation.

So far, so good. Yet seldom are Nepal-India relations so straightforward. Take the two major deals struck this time. After the 2015 earthquakes, India extended Nepal a $750 million line of credit. Yet due to the stringent conditions placed by the Indian side – including the mandatory use of Indian manpower and material for some post-quake construction projects – much of this sum was never spent. The new line of credit could face similar hurdles.

Even the new deal for an air-entry route over Bhairahawa faces hurdles. In 2016, there was a similar agreement to open Mahendranagar in Western Nepal as an air-entry point. Yet the deal was scrapped as Nepal-India relations soured. For the Bhairahawa route, the two sides have yet to settle technical details like permissible aircraft altitudes.

Then there is geopolitics. Long suspicious of the Shah government’s supposed pro-Western tilt and its recent shift toward New Delhi, Beijing is already complaining about Kathmandu’s apparent reluctance to implement pending bilateral agreements hammered out under the Belt and Road Initiative framework. Shah, who came to power on a populist and nationalist plank, could face a backlash if he is seen as neglecting China. Maintaining a careful balance between Beijing and New Delhi has always been a central pillar of Nepal’s foreign policy conduct.

Moreover, Nepal did not get everything it asked for during Shah’s trip. It would have preferred Mahendranagar to Bhairahawa as an air entry point. India also declined to discuss pending border issues.

The visit was undoubtedly shaped by short-term calculations on both sides. For Modi, in light of strained ties with most South Asian countries, the immediate goal was to show that India under his leadership can still cultivate friends in the neighborhood. Shah, for his part, desperately sought international financial help to rebuild his flood-ravaged country.

It remains to be seen whether the two sides will look beyond their short-term interests and pursue the long-term partnership outlined in their joint vision document, “Developed India and Prosperous Nepal: Reimagining Partnership.”

Whatever the case, the eventual agreements mattered, as did the symbolism of a young prime minister’s maiden, largely controversy-free bilateral trip to the south. On those counts, Shah’s India visit was a success.
